prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "ROYAL BANK OF CANADA" (ticker RY), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "RY", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: Royal Bank of Canada
markets: Canadian personal banking (mortgages, deposits, credit cards)
Wealth management and asset management (Canada, US via RBC Wealth Management and City National, UK)
Global capital markets and investment banking

mission.statement: Helping clients thrive and communities prosper.
mission.source: RBC website, Purpose, Vision and Values page (rbc.com/our-company)
mission.plain: RBC wants to help its customers do well with their money and help the places they live do well too.

about.plain: RBC is Canada's biggest bank. It keeps people's savings safe, lends money for homes, cars and businesses, and gives out credit cards. It also helps rich families and pension funds invest, helps big companies raise money on stock and bond markets, and sells insurance. It makes money from the gap between the interest it pays savers and charges borrowers, plus fees.
about.customers: More than 19 million people, businesses, governments and institutions, mostly in Canada and the US.
about.everyday: Millions of Canadians use an RBC debit card, mortgage or Avion rewards credit card, and see its blue-and-gold lion logo on bank branches and ATMs.

money.plain: Mortgages, savings accounts, credit cards and car loans for households
Investment advice, mutual funds and private banking for wealthy clients in Canada, the US and UK
Investment banking, trading and lending to big companies and governments
Loans, deposits and payments for small and mid-sized businesses
Life, health, creditor and travel insurance and reinsurance
Clients of HSBC Canada, bought for C$13.5 billion and closed March 28, 2024, folded into RBC's segments

result.summary: RBC has a durable competitive advantage: it is the largest bank in a five-bank Canadian oligopoly protected by strict regulation, with a cheap, sticky deposit base and the top scale in Canadian wealth management and capital markets. That shows in FY2025 net income of C$20,369M on C$66,605M of revenue (a 30.6% net margin) and a 16.3% ROE, rising to 17.5% in the first nine months of FY2026. Its advantage is strongest in Canada; in the US and global markets it is a mid-sized player.

pricingPower.evidence: Canada's concentrated banking market lets RBC hold fees and spreads without losing clients: FY2025 revenue rose 16.2% to C$66,605M while non-interest expense rose only 6.8% to C$36,592M, and nine-month FY2026 revenue rose another 9.2%; but loan and deposit pricing ultimately follows Bank of Canada rates and competition from TD, the other big banks and digital challengers.

moats.evidence: RBC, founded in 1864, is Canada's largest bank by market value and widely seen as its safest and most trusted; the brand anchors its lead in Canadian retail, wealth (RBC Dominion Securities, RBC Global Asset Management) and investment banking.

Clients holding mortgages, chequing accounts, credit cards, investments and payroll at one bank rarely move; RBC's Avion rewards and bundled products deepen this stickiness across its 19+ million clients.
Its large branch and ATM network and Interac/payments role give modest convenience benefits, but banking has few true network effects.

As the biggest Canadian bank (C$2,498,817M of assets at July 31, 2026) RBC spreads technology, compliance and marketing costs over the largest revenue base; its FY2025 net margin of 30.6% topped BMO (24.1%), CIBC (29.0%) and Scotiabank (20.6%).
Canada's market is served by five large banks under tight OSFI regulation and foreign-ownership limits, leaving little room for new entrants to reach scale.
RBC is the incumbent; it is the one being counter-positioned by low-fee digital players such as Wealthsimple and EQ Bank rather than the reverse.
Decades of conservative credit underwriting and risk management, plus an early AI investment through Borealis AI (founded 2016), give it operating know-how that peers have struggled to match.
Its banking licence and low-cost Canadian deposit base (C$1,644,573M of deposits at July 31, 2026) are valuable but shared with the other big banks rather than exclusive.

customers.evidence: RBC serves more than 19 million clients and keeps them through bundled products and Avion rewards, but like all big Canadian banks it draws public complaints about fees and service, and no strong independent NPS lead is published.

talent.evidence: With 96,628 full-time-equivalent employees at October 31, 2025, RBC is one of Canada's largest and most sought-after employers in finance and technology, and its Borealis AI lab and RBC Capital Markets help it recruit top graduates.

product.evidence: RBC's products are solid rather than unique, but it is a recognised leader in bank AI adoption, ranked near the top of the Evident AI Index of global banks, and its wealth and capital markets franchises are Canada's largest.

competitors.name: Toronto-Dominion Bank
competitors.note: Canada's other giant in retail, commercial banking, wealth and cards; also a large US retail bank.

competitors.name: Bank of Montreal
competitors.note: Canadian and US commercial and personal banking, wealth and capital markets.

competitors.name: Bank of Nova Scotia
competitors.note: Canadian personal and commercial banking, wealth and capital markets; Latin America.

competitors.name: Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce
competitors.note: Canadian personal, commercial and wealth banking; mortgages and cards.

competitors.name: National Bank of Canada
competitors.note: Strong in Quebec retail and commercial banking, wealth and capital markets; bought Canadian Western Bank in 2025.

competitors.name: Desjardins Group
competitors.note: Large Quebec-based co-operative in personal banking and insurance.

competitors.name: Sun Life Financial
competitors.note: Canadian insurance, group benefits and asset management.

competitors.name: JPMorgan Chase
competitors.note: Global investment banking, trading and US wealth management.

competitors.name: Morgan Stanley
competitors.note: US wealth management (vs RBC Wealth Management US) and capital markets.

competitors.name: Wells Fargo
competitors.note: US commercial and private banking, competing with City National in California.

competitors.name: Wealthsimple
competitors.note: Low-cost Canadian digital investing and banking app targeting younger clients.

competitors.name: EQB (EQ Bank)
competitors.note: Canadian digital bank competing for deposits and mortgages.

marketShare.market: Revenue of Canada's Big Five banks (RBC, TD, BMO, Scotiabank, CIBC)
marketShare.measure: share of combined reported FY2025 total revenue (C$237,530M), calculated from each bank's FY2025 earnings release

threats: A Canadian housing downturn or recession (worsened by US tariffs) hitting its large mortgage and commercial loan books; PCL rose to C$4,362M in FY2025 from C$3,232M.
Falling interest rates and deposit competition squeezing net interest margins.
Digital challengers such as Wealthsimple, EQ Bank and open banking eroding fees and deposit share among younger Canadians.
Execution and regulatory risk in its US operations (City National, RBC Wealth Management US) and in capital markets trading.
Tighter OSFI capital rules or political pressure on bank fees and profits in Canada.

ceo.name: David (Dave) McKay
ceo.background: Joined RBC in 1988 as a co-op student and spent his career there; Bachelor of Mathematics (computer science) from the University of Waterloo and MBA from Ivey Business School

c1.evidence: RBC leads Canadian banking, a mature, slow-growing industry, not an emerging one.

c2.evidence: Clients choose RBC for its scale, safety and full product range, and Canada's five-bank oligopoly plus high switching costs make that advantage likely to last for decades.

c3.evidence: Nearly every Canadian knows RBC and it is the default leader in Canadian banking and wealth, but it is little known to ordinary people outside Canada and few customers enthuse about a bank.

c4.evidence: RBC repeats its purpose 'Helping clients thrive and communities prosper' and backs it with programs like RBC Foundation and RBC Future Launch, but management is mainly judged on ROE and earnings.

c6.evidence: “big, safe, trusted, expensive fees”: Canadians see RBC as the country's largest and most solid bank, an impression that is mostly positive despite usual complaints about bank fees.

c7.evidence: Banking and wealth management are huge markets growing with the economy and wealth accumulation, but they are not riding a fast secular trend like AI or cloud.

c8.evidence: RBC can keep growing in US wealth and commercial banking (City National) and global capital markets, but its name and business model tie it to banking.

m1.evidence: McKay pushed RBC early into digital banking and AI (Borealis AI, 2016) and talks of a data-driven bank, but his vision is evolutionary rather than transformative.

m2.evidence: McKay is a career RBC lifer since 1988 and CEO since 2014 who manages for the long term, but he is a professional steward, not a founder.

m4.evidence: RBC emphasises 'Client First' as a core value and invests in employee programs, but there is no strong public evidence of exceptional servant leadership.

m5.evidence: McKay built an innovation culture unusual for a bank (Borealis AI, NOMI insights, RBC Ventures), though RBC remains a conservative incumbent.

m6.evidence: McKay holds a computer science degree from Waterloo, started at RBC in technology roles and is known for personally championing its digital and AI agenda.

m7.evidence: McKay has led RBC's community programs and Canadian youth and climate initiatives, but its 2024 dismissal of CFO Nadine Ahn over an undisclosed relationship showed governance lapses below him.

m7b.evidence: No record found of McKay giving a commencement speech at Stanford, Harvard, MIT or a similar top university.

m8b.evidence: McKay has a measured, low-key banker's public persona rather than a distinctive celebrity personality.

m9.evidence: Under McKay, net income rose from C$11,437M in FY2020 to C$20,369M in FY2025, he closed and integrated the C$13.5B HSBC Canada deal, and ROE reached 17.5% in the first nine months of FY2026.

m10.evidence: RBC is not known for frugality; non-interest expense was C$36,592M in FY2025 and the CEO is among Canada's highest-paid executives.

c10.evidence: RBC safely holds savings and funds homes and businesses for over 19 million clients, important but mostly in Canada and not life-changing on a global scale.

p2.evidence: Running a C$2.5 trillion bank safely is hard and vital to Canada's economy, but the product is one many large banks provide.

f1.evidence: Revenue rose from C$47,181M in FY2020 to C$66,605M in FY2025, with one dip in FY2022 (C$48,985M vs C$49,693M in FY2021).

f2.evidence: Net margin went from 24.2% in FY2020 to 30.6% in FY2025 but swung in between (32.3% in FY2021); gross margin is not meaningful for a bank.

f3.evidence: As a bank RBC is heavily leveraged (total liabilities C$2,353,723M vs equity C$145,094M at July 31, 2026), but its CET1 ratio of 13.5% is well above regulatory minimums and equity is positive.

f4.evidence: Net income rose from C$11,437M (FY2020) to C$20,369M (FY2025) with a dip to C$14,866M in FY2023; bank operating cash flow swings with deposits and trading and is not a useful trend.

v1.evidence: RBC is a strong all-round bank, but there is no single practical reason an ordinary person would pick it over TD or the other big banks, whose products are similar.

v2.evidence: With about 96,600 FTE employees, RBC is a well-regarded Canadian employer and graduate recruiter, but it does not top global best-workplace rankings.

c5.evidence: If RBC vanished, millions of Canadians would lose their bank, mortgage lender and adviser and markets would be disrupted, but other big banks could absorb its customers over time.
